claim: The concurrent application of subtoxic doses of soluble oligomeric forms of human amyloid-beta (oAβ) and Tau (oTau) proteins impairs memory and its electrophysiological surrogate long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: The concurrent application of subtoxic doses of soluble oligomeric forms of human amyloid-beta (oAβ) and Tau (oTau) proteins impairs memory and its electrophysiological surrogate long-term potentiation (LTP), effects that may be mediated by intra-neuronal oligomers uptake.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Fá et al., 2016) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: oTau can bind to amyloid precursor protein (APP).
source: We found that as already shown for oAβ, also oTau can bind to amyloid precursor protein (APP).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation and far-Western blot experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Efficient intra-neuronal uptake of oAβ and oTau requires expression of APP.
source: Moreover, efficient intra-neuronal uptake of oAβ and oTau requires expression of APP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cultured hippocampal neurons showing reduced oligomer internalization in APP-KO cells compared to WT cells (Figure 2).

claim: The toxic effect of both extracellular oAβ and oTau on memory and LTP is dependent upon APP.
source: Finally, the toxic effect of both extracellular oAβ and oTau on memory and LTP is dependent upon APP since APP-KO mice were resistant to oAβ- and oTau-induced defects in spatial/associative memory and LTP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests (Figures 3 and 4) and electrophysiological recordings (Figure 5) in APP-KO mice.

claim: APP might serve as a common therapeutic target against Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative diseases characterized by abnormal levels of Aβ and/or Tau.
source: Thus, APP might serve as a common therapeutic target against Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and a host of other neurodegenerative diseases characterized by abnormal levels of Aβ and/or Tau.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental findings showing APP-dependence of oAβ and oTau toxicity.

claim: Protein aggregation and deposition are key pathogenetic processes in several neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease (AD), tauopathies, Parkinson's Disease, Huntington disease and many others.
source: Protein aggregation and deposition have been considered key pathogenetic processes in several neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's Disease (AD), tauopathies, Parkinson's Disease, Huntington disease and many others (Shelkovnikova et al., 2012; Takalo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Shelkovnikova et al., 2012; Takalo et al., 2013).

claim: Soluble small aggregates of proteins have gained attention in studies aimed at understanding the etiopathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: More recently, soluble small aggregates of these proteins have gained a lot of attention in studies aimed at understanding the etiopathogenesis of these diseases.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and trends in the field.

claim: The abnormal increases of the levels of amyloid-beta (Aβ) and Tau proteins and their aggregation are crucial steps in the chain of events leading to dementia in AD.
source: This is particularly evident in AD, in which the abnormal increases of the levels of amyloid-beta (Aβ) and Tau proteins and their aggregation are crucial steps in the chain of events leading to dementia (Irvine et al., 2008; Kopeikina et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Irvine et al., 2008; Kopeikina et al., 2012).

claim: Soluble oligomeric forms of Aβ (oAβ) and Tau (oTau) are present in human cerebrospinal fluid in healthy individuals and, in higher amounts, in AD patients.
source: The importance of soluble oligomeric forms of Aβ (oAβ) and Tau (oTau) has been corroborated by numerous evidences demonstrating their presence in human cerebrospinal fluid in healthy individuals and, in higher amounts, in AD patients (Hölttä et al., 2013; Sengupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Hölttä et al., 2013; Sengupta et al., 2017).

claim: oAβ and oTau disrupt synaptic plasticity, paving the way to subsequent cognitive impairment.
source: oAβ and oTau are also toxic to cell-to-cell communication, as they disrupt synaptic plasticity, paving the way to the subsequent cognitive impairment (Selkoe, 2008; Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2012; Fá et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Selkoe, 2008; Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2012; Fá et al., 2016).

claim: A brief exposure to a combination of subtoxic doses of extracellular oAβ and oTau dramatically reduces memory and its electrophysiological surrogate long-term potentiation (LTP).
source: Interestingly, we have recently demonstrated that a brief exposure to a combination of subtoxic doses of extracellular oAβ and oTau dramatically reduces memory and its electrophysiological surrogate long-term potentiation (LTP) (Fá et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Fá et al., 2016).

claim: Aβ and Tau can form insoluble deposits: extracellular amyloid plaques due to the accumulation of Aβ, and intracellular insoluble filaments and neurofibrillary tangles formed by Tau.
source: Both proteins can form insoluble deposits: that is, extracellular amyloid plaques due to the accumulation of Aβ, and intracellular insoluble filaments and neurofibrillary tangles formed by Tau.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about AD pathology.

claim: Aβ and Tau are present as non-fibrillar soluble monomeric and oligomeric species.
source: In addition, Aβ and Tau are present as non-fibrillar soluble monomeric and oligomeric species (Selkoe, 2008; Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2010; Fá et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Selkoe, 2008; Lasagna-Reeves et al., 2010; Fá et al., 2016).

claim: Aβ and Tau can be secreted at the synapse in an activity-dependent fashion.
source: They can be secreted at the synapse in an activity-dependent fashion (Kamenetz et al., 2003; Pooler et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2014; Fá et al., 2016), and enter neurons (Frost et al., 2009; Lai and McLaurin, 2010; Wu et al. 2013; Fá et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Kamenetz et al., 2003; Pooler et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2014; Fá et al., 2016).

claim: Aβ and Tau can enter neurons.
source: They can be secreted at the synapse in an activity-dependent fashion (Kamenetz et al., 2003; Pooler et al., 2013; Yamada et al., 2014; Fá et al., 2016), and enter neurons (Frost et al., 2009; Lai and McLaurin, 2010; Wu et al. 2013; Fá et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Frost et al., 2009; Lai and McLaurin, 2010; Wu et al. 2013; Fá et al., 2016).

claim: Both Aβ and Tau can bind to amyloid precursor protein (APP).
source: Moreover, both Aβ and Tau can bind to amyloid precursor protein (APP) (Lorenzo et al., 2000; Van Nostrand et al., 2002; Shaked et al., 2006; Fogel et al., 2014; Takahashi et al., 2015), a protein with a central role in AD pathogenesis that might act as a cell surface receptor (Deyts et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Lorenzo et al., 2000; Van Nostrand et al., 2002; Shaked et al., 2006; Fogel et al., 2014; Takahashi et al., 2015).

claim: APP has a central role in AD pathogenesis and might act as a cell surface receptor.
source: Moreover, both Aβ and Tau can bind to amyloid precursor protein (APP) (Lorenzo et al., 2000; Van Nostrand et al., 2002; Shaked et al., 2006; Fogel et al., 2014; Takahashi et al., 2015), a protein with a central role in AD pathogenesis that might act as a cell surface receptor (Deyts et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Deyts et al., 2016).

claim: APP is the precursor of Aβ, which derives from sequential cleavage of APP by β-secretase (also known as BACE1) and γ-secretase.
source: APP, the precursor of Aβ, which derives from sequential cleavage of APP by β-secretase (also known as BACE1) and γ-secretase (Cole and Vassar, 2007; De Strooper, 2007), has a central role in AD pathogenesis and might act as both an Aβ precursor and a cell surface receptor (Deyts et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Cole and Vassar, 2007; De Strooper, 2007).

claim: Different species of Aβ (monomers, dimers, oligomers and fibrils) bind to APP.
source: The interaction between oAβ and APP has been thoroughly investigated in studies demonstrating that different species of Aβ (monomers, dimers, oligomers and fibrils) bind to APP (Lorenzo et al., 2000; Van Nostrand et al., 2002; Shaked et al., 2006; Fogel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Lorenzo et al., 2000; Van Nostrand et al., 2002; Shaked et al., 2006; Fogel et al., 2014).

claim: Previous studies on Tau-APP binding did not use oligomers but fibrils.
source: However, there is no proof that oTau binds to APP, as previous studies on Tau-APP binding did not use oligomers but fibrils (Giaccone et al., 1996; Islam and Levy, 1997; Smith et al., 1995; Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Giaccone et al., 1996; Islam and Levy, 1997; Smith et al., 1995; Takahashi et al., 2015).

claim: APP co-immunoprecipitated with oTau in HEK293 cells stably transfected with human APP with the Swedish mutation.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, APP co-IPed oTau.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A from co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: In lysates from WT cultures, oTau was detected at the molecular weight of APP (~110 KDa) by an anti-Tau antibody (Tau 5).
source: We found that, in lysates from WT cultures, oTau (used as the bait protein) was detected at the molecular weight of APP (~110 KDa) by an anti-Tau antibody (Tau 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from far-Western blot experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The band at the molecular weight of APP was not observed in lysates from control APP-KO cultures in far-Western blot experiments.
source: Conversely, this band was not observed in lysates from control APP-KO cultures (Figure 1B), supporting the interaction between murine APP and oTau.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from far-Western blot experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 91 ± 3% of WT MAP2-positive cells exhibited Aβ accumulation after extracellular oAβ−555 application.
source: Aβ accumulation was found in 91 ± 3% of WT MAP2-positive cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1) and the mean number of intracellular fluorescent spots/neuron was 5.3 ± 0.4 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean number of intracellular fluorescent Aβ spots per WT neuron was 5.3 ± 0.4.
source: Aβ accumulation was found in 91 ± 3% of WT MAP2-positive cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1) and the mean number of intracellular fluorescent spots/neuron was 5.3 ± 0.4 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 73 ± 5% of APP-KO cells internalized Aβ after extracellular oAβ−555 application.
source: When the same treatment was applied to APP-KO cultures we found that 73 ± 5% of total cells internalized Aβ (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1) and the mean number of fluorescent spots was 2.9 ± 0.2 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The mean number of intracellular fluorescent Aβ spots per APP-KO neuron was 2.9 ± 0.2.
source: When the same treatment was applied to APP-KO cultures we found that 73 ± 5% of total cells internalized Aβ (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1) and the mean number of fluorescent spots was 2.9 ± 0.2 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 80 ± 6% of WT cells internalized oTau-IRIS5 containing 2.7 ± 0.2 fluorescent spots.
source: Similar results were obtained when WT and APP-KO neurons were treated with extracellular oTau-IRIS5 (Figure 2D) which was found in 80 ± 6% of WT cells containing 2.7 ± 0.2 fluorescent spots and in 47 ± 6% of APP-KO neurons exhibiting 1.4 ± 0.1 spots (Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: 47 ± 6% of APP-KO neurons internalized oTau-IRIS5 exhibiting 1.4 ± 0.1 spots.
source: Similar results were obtained when WT and APP-KO neurons were treated with extracellular oTau-IRIS5 (Figure 2D) which was found in 80 ± 6% of WT cells containing 2.7 ± 0.2 fluorescent spots and in 47 ± 6% of APP-KO neurons exhibiting 1.4 ± 0.1 spots (Figure 2E–F, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: The internalization index showed a 61% reduction in APP-KO neurons compared to WT cells for oAβ.
source: Moreover, to provide a global estimate of the protein uploading into neurons, we performed quantitative analysis of these data through the 'internalization index', which showed a 61% reduction in APP-KO neurons compared to WT cells for oAβ (Figure 2G, Figure 2—source data 3), and a 69% reduction for oTau (Figure 2H, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The internalization index showed a 69% reduction in APP-KO neurons compared to WT cells for oTau.
source: Moreover, to provide a global estimate of the protein uploading into neurons, we performed quantitative analysis of these data through the 'internalization index', which showed a 61% reduction in APP-KO neurons compared to WT cells for oAβ (Figure 2G, Figure 2—source data 3), and a 69% reduction for oTau (Figure 2H, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The amounts of Aβ and tau oligomers attached to neuronal surface did not significantly differ between WT and APP-KO cells.
source: Notably, the amounts of Aβ and tau oligomers attached to neuronal surface did not significantly differ between WT and APP-KO cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: Fluorescent Aβ spots attached to neuronal surface were 6.9 ± 0.5 and 6.5 ± 0.6 for WT and APP-KO, respectively.
source: Specifically, fluorescent Aβ spots were 6.9 ± 0.5 and 6.5 ± 0.6 for WT and APP-KO, respectively (Figure 2I, Figure 2—source data 4); whereas for Tau they were 4.3 ± 0.4 and 4.0 ± 0.4, respectively (Figure 2J, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Fluorescent Tau spots attached to neuronal surface were 4.3 ± 0.4 and 4.0 ± 0.4 for WT and APP-KO, respectively.
source: Specifically, fluorescent Aβ spots were 6.9 ± 0.5 and 6.5 ± 0.6 for WT and APP-KO, respectively (Figure 2I, Figure 2—source data 4); whereas for Tau they were 4.3 ± 0.4 and 4.0 ± 0.4, respectively (Figure 2J, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: APP suppression reduces the entrance of extracellular oligomers of both Aβ and Tau into neurons.
source: Collectively, these data show that APP suppression reduces the entrance of extracellular oligomers of both Aβ and Tau into neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing reduced internalization in APP-KO neurons (Figure 2).

claim: Neuronal uploading of oAβ from the extracellular space reduces LTP.
source: Neuronal uploading of oAβ from the extracellular space reduces LTP (Ripoli et al., 2014), a cellular surrogate of memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Ripoli et al., 2014).

claim: Both associative fear memory and spatial memory are impaired by oAβ.
source: Interestingly, both associative fear memory and spatial memory, two types of memory that are altered in AD patients, are impaired by oAβ (Puzzo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Puzzo et al., 2014).

claim: High doses of oAβ (200 nM) infused into the dorsal mouse hippocampi resulted in reduced freezing 24 hr after the electric shock in WT mice.
source: Consisting with previous results (Fiorito et al., 2013; Watterson et al., 2013), high doses of oAβ (200 nM in a final volume of 1 µl, one injection 20 min prior to the training) infused via bilateral cannulas into the dorsal mouse hippocampi, resulted in reduced freezing 24 hr after the electric shock in WT mice (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1), confirming that contextual fear memory is altered by high amounts of oAβ.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning tests shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Memory was spared by the deleterious effects of oAβ in APP-KO mice.
source: By contrast, in interleaved experiments, memory was spared by the deleterious effects of oAβ in APP-KO mice (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning tests shown in Figure 3A.

claim: APP-KO mice that were infused with vehicle displayed normal memory.
source: Similarly, APP-KO mice that were infused with vehicle displayed normal memory, as previously shown in KO animals of this age (Senechal et al., 2008) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning tests shown in Figure 3A and citation to previous literature (Senechal et al., 2008).

claim: Cued fear learning was not affected in both WT and APP-KO animals treated with vehicle or oAβ.
source: We also confirmed that the defect in contextual memory found in WT mice was due to an oAβ-induced hippocampal impairment, whereas cued fear learning, a type of learning depending upon amygdala function (Phillips and LeDoux, 1992), was not affected in both WT and APP-KO animals treated with vehicle or oAβ (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cued fear conditioning tests shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sensory threshold assessment did not reveal any difference among the four groups of mice in fear conditioning experiments.
source: Moreover, we excluded that the defect was due to deficits in mouse capability to perceive the electric shock, as sensory threshold assessment did not reveal any difference among the four groups of mice (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sensory threshold assessment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: WT mice infused with oAβ (200 nM) made a higher number of errors than vehicle-infused WT littermates during the second day of RAWM testing.
source: As previously shown (Watterson et al., 2013), WT mice infused with oAβ (200 nM in a final volume of 1 µl, one injection 20 min prior to the first trial of RAWM training in day one and two, bilaterally) made a higher number of errors than vehicle-infused WT littermates during the second day of RAWM testing (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RAWM tests shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The performance of APP-KO mice in RAWM was not affected by oAβ infusion.
source: By contrast, the performance of APP-KO mice, which was normal when these animals were infused with vehicle, was not affected by the Aβ infusion (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RAWM tests shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Control trials with a visible platform did not show any difference in speed or latency to reach the platform among the four groups in RAWM testing.
source: Control trials with a visible platform did not show any difference in speed or latency to reach the platform among the four groups, indicating that oAβ infusion did not affect the motility, vision and motivation of mice during RAWM testing (Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from visible platform tests shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Open field testing did not reveal any difference among WT and APP-KO mice treated with vehicle or oAβ.
source: Moreover, open field testing did not reveal any difference among WT and APP-KO mice treated with vehicle or oAβ, indicating that mouse exploratory behavior, which might affect animal performance in the memory task, was not affected by treatment or genotype (Figure 3G–H, Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field tests shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: The deleterious effect exerted by oAβ on memory is dependent upon the presence of endogenous APP.
source: Collectively, these experiments indicate that the deleterious effect exerted by oAβ on memory is dependent upon the presence of endogenous APP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that APP-KO mice are resistant to oAβ-induced memory deficits (Figure 3).

claim: Both associative fear memory and spatial memory are impaired by oTau.
source: Both associative fear memory and spatial memory are impaired not only by oAβ, but also by oTau (Fá et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Fá et al., 2016).

claim: oTau infusion (500 nM) affected contextual fear memory and spatial memory in WT animals.
source: As previously demonstrated (Fá et al., 2016), oTau infusion (500 nM in a final volume of 1 µl, two injections bilaterally at 180 and 20 min prior to the electric shock for fear conditioning or the first trial of the RAWM training in day one and two) affected the two forms of memory in WT animals (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning and RAWM tests shown in Figure 4A and 4D.

claim: APP-KO mice displayed normal performance when they were infused with oTau both in the fear conditioning and RAWM tests.
source: By contrast, APP-KO mice displayed normal performance when they were infused with oTau both in the fear conditioning and RAWM tests (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1 and Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fear conditioning and RAWM tests shown in Figure 4A and 4D.

claim: No behavioral differences were observed between groups of mice tested for cued conditioning, sensory threshold, visible platform or open field in oTau experiments.
source: Moreover, we did not observe any behavioral differences between groups of mice tested for cued conditioning (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1), sensory threshold (Figure, Figure 4—source data 1), visible platform (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—source data 2) or open field (Figure 4G and H, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from control behavioral tests shown in Figure 4B, 4C, 4E, 4F, 4G, and 4H.

claim: The impairment of memory induced by oTau was dependent upon the presence of APP.
source: Thus, as for oAβ, the impairment of memory induced by oTau was dependent upon the presence of APP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that APP-KO mice are resistant to oTau-induced memory deficits (Figure 4).

claim: LTP is reduced after treatment with both high amounts of oAβ and/or oTau.
source: LTP represents a cellular correlate of learning and memory (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993). It is reduced after treatment with both high amounts of oAβ and/or oTau (Fá et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Fá et al., 2016).

claim: Basal synaptic transmission did not reveal any difference between WT and APP-KO slices.
source: Following recording of basal synaptic transmission (BST), which did not reveal any difference between WT and APP-KO slices (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1), slices were perfused with oAβ, or oTau, or vehicle prior to eliciting LTP through a theta-burst stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Perfusion with oAβ (200 nM for 20 min before the tetanus) reduced LTP in slices from WT mice.
source: As previously demonstrated (Puzzo et al., 2005), perfusion with oAβ (200 nM for 20 min before the tetanus) reduced LTP in slices from WT mice (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5B.

claim: oAβ did not impair LTP in slices from APP-KO littermates.
source: However, consistent with the behavioral results, the peptide did not impair LTP in slices from APP-KO littermates (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5B.

claim: oTau (100 nM for 20 min before tetanus) reduced LTP in WT slices but not in APP-KO slices.
source: Similarly, oTau (100 nM for 20 min before tetanus) reduced LTP in WT slices but not in APP-KO slices (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Basal synaptic transmission at the CA3-CA1 connection in slices from 3- to 4-month-old BACE1-KO mice was similar to WT littermates.
source: BST recording did not reveal any difference between WT and BACE1-KO slices (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5D.

claim: oAβ and oTau reduced LTP in slices from BACE1-KO mice similar to WT mice.
source: Slices perfusion with oAβ (200 nM for 20 min before the tetanus), or oTau (100 nM for 20 min before tetanus), or vehicle showed that, similar to WT mice, oAβ and oTau reduced LTP in slices from BACE1-KO mice (Figure 5E, Figure 5—source data 5 and Figure 5F, Figure 5—source data 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claim: APP processing is not involved in the toxicity of extracellularly-applied Aβ and Tau.
source: Thus, these experiments demonstrate that APP processing is not involved in the toxicity of extracellularly-applied Aβ and Tau.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that BACE1-KO mice are susceptible to oAβ and oTau toxicity (Figure 5E-F).

claim: Human amylin (Amy) is an amyloid protein of 37 amino-acids differing from Aβ42 in its primary sequence, but sharing with it the ability to form β-sheets and oligomerize.
source: To address this question, we selected human amylin (Amy), an amyloid protein of 37 amino-acids differing from Aβ42 in its primary sequence, but sharing with it the ability to form β-sheets and oligomerize (Wineman-Fisher et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Wineman-Fisher et al., 2016).

claim: Amy crosses the blood brain barrier.
source: Amy crosses the blood brain barrier (Banks et al., 1995), and has a profile of neurotoxicity that is strikingly similar to that of Aβ (Jhamandas et al., 2011), including the marked reduction of LTP (Kimura et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Banks et al., 1995).

claim: Amy has a profile of neurotoxicity that is strikingly similar to that of Aβ.
source: Amy crosses the blood brain barrier (Banks et al., 1995), and has a profile of neurotoxicity that is strikingly similar to that of Aβ (Jhamandas et al., 2011), including the marked reduction of LTP (Kimura et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Jhamandas et al., 2011).

claim: Amy produces a marked reduction of LTP.
source: Amy crosses the blood brain barrier (Banks et al., 1995), and has a profile of neurotoxicity that is strikingly similar to that of Aβ (Jhamandas et al., 2011), including the marked reduction of LTP (Kimura et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Kimura et al., 2012).

claim: Perfusion of hippocampal slices for 20 min with 200 nM oligomeric Amy (oAmy) produced a marked reduction of LTP in WT slices.
source: As previously demonstrated (Kimura et al., 2012), perfusion of hippocampal slices for 20 min with 200 nM oligomeric Amy (oAmy) produced a marked reduction of LTP in WT slices (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The same impairment of LTP by oAmy was observed in slices from APP-KO mice.
source: The same impairment of LTP was observed in slices from APP-KO mice (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 7); thus, different than oTau and oAβ, oAmy does not require APP for its negative effect on synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5G.

claim: oAmy does not require APP for its negative effect on synaptic plasticity.
source: The same impairment of LTP was observed in slices from APP-KO mice (Figure 5G, Figure 5—source data 7); thus, different than oTau and oAβ, oAmy does not require APP for its negative effect on synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that oAmy impairs LTP in APP-KO slices (Figure 5G).

claim: A brief exposure to both oAβ or oTau, but not oAmy, needs the presence of endogenous APP to impair LTP.
source: Collectively, these experiments suggest that a brief exposure to both oAβ or oTau, but not oAmy, needs the presence of endogenous APP to impair LTP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing the effects of oAβ, oTau, and oAmy in WT and APP-KO slices (Figure 5).

claim: Oligomers of proteins are likely to be involved in the cell-to-cell propagation of the pathology in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Oligomers of these proteins are gaining a lot of attention because they are likely to be involved in the cell-to-cell propagation of the pathology, and look more acutely toxic than large insoluble aggregates.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge in the field of neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Oligomers look more acutely toxic than large insoluble aggregates.
source: Oligomers of these proteins are gaining a lot of attention because they are likely to be involved in the cell-to-cell propagation of the pathology, and look more acutely toxic than large insoluble aggregates.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge in the field of neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: In AD, oligomers of both Aβ and Tau produce an immediate reduction of synaptic plasticity and memory when extracellularly applied.
source: For instance, in AD, oligomers of both Aβ and Tau have been shown to produce an immediate reduction of synaptic plasticity and memory when extracellularly applied (Fá et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Fá et al., 2016).

claim: The negative effects of oAβ and oTau occurred not only with high concentrations of Aβ or Tau alone, but also when sub-toxic doses of oAβ were combined with sub-toxic doses of oTau.
source: Intriguingly, the negative effects of oAβ and oTau occurred not only with high concentrations of Aβ or Tau alone, but also when sub-toxic doses of oAβ were combined with sub-toxic doses of oTau (Fá et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Fá et al., 2016).

claim: The suppression of APP causes a marked reduction of the oligomer entrance into neurons.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the suppression of APP, to which both oAβ and oTau can bind, causes a marked reduction of the oligomer entrance into neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing reduced internalization in APP-KO neurons (Figure 2).

claim: There is a common mechanism of action for extracellular Aβ and Tau oligomers, whose deleterious effect on LTP and memory depends upon the presence of endogenous APP.
source: Most importantly, we have found a common mechanism of action for extracellular Aβ and Tau oligomers, whose deleterious effect on LTP and memory depends upon the presence of endogenous APP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that APP-KO mice are resistant to both oAβ and oTau toxicity (Figures 3, 4, and 5).

claim: Extracellular oAβ requires APP to impair synaptic plasticity and memory.
source: Our finding that extracellular oAβ requires APP to impair synaptic plasticity and memory is consistent with previous studies showing that Aβ neurotoxicity might be mediated by APP, as suggested by the reduced vulnerability towards Aβ of cultured APP null neurons or mutated APP cells (Lorenzo et al., 2000; Shaked et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study (Figures 3 and 5) and citations to previous literature (Lorenzo et al., 2000; Shaked et al., 2006).

claim: The presence of APP is likely to contribute to hippocampal hyperactivity, which has been suggested as a key mechanism of disease etiopathogenesis both in AD animal models and patients.
source: This finding is also consistent with the observation that the presence of APP is likely to contribute to hippocampal hyperactivity, which has been suggested as a key mechanism of disease etiopathogenesis both in AD animal models and patients (Bakker et al., 2012; Busche et al., 2012; Palop et al., 2007; Verret et al., 2012; Vossel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Bakker et al., 2012; Busche et al., 2012; Palop et al., 2007; Verret et al., 2012; Vossel et al., 2013).

claim: APP has been demonstrated to bind Aβ monomers and dimers leading to activity-dependent APP-APP conformational changes that enhance neurotransmitter release.
source: Along with these studies, APP has been demonstrated to bind Aβ monomers and dimers leading to activity-dependent APP-APP conformational changes that enhance neurotransmitter release (Fogel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Fogel et al., 2014).

claim: When Aβ is accumulating in the brain, the increase of release probability might induce hippocampal hyperactivity resulting in failure of synaptic plasticity and memory loss.
source: When Aβ is accumulating in the brain, this increase of release probability might induce hippocampal hyperactivity resulting in failure of synaptic plasticity and memory loss (Koppensteiner et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Koppensteiner et al., 2016) and involves speculative reasoning about mechanisms.

claim: APP has been involved in the uptake of Tau fibrils into cells influencing Tau intracellular aggregation and spreading in the brain.
source: Moreover, recently, APP has been involved in the uptake of Tau fibrils into cells influencing Tau intracellular aggregation and spreading in the brain (Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Takahashi et al., 2015).

claim: APP is a key molecule involved in a common mechanism by which extracellular oAβ and oTau interfere with second messenger cascades relevant to memory formation.
source: The dependence for the presence of APP shared by both oAβ and oTau in order to impair synaptic plasticity, suggests that APP is a key molecule involved in a common mechanism by which extracellular oAβ and oTau interfere with second messenger cascades relevant to memory formation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing APP-dependence of both oAβ and oTau toxicity.

claim: Aβ and Tau share numerous biochemical characteristics and previous studies have suggested a possible common toxicity mechanism.
source: Indeed, Aβ and Tau share numerous biochemical characteristics and previous studies have suggested a possible common toxicity mechanism (Gendreau et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Gendreau et al., 2013).

claim: Both Aβ and Tau are β-sheet forming proteins, which explains their propensity for oligomerization and close association with membrane.
source: Both peptides are β-sheet forming proteins, which explains their propensity for oligomerization and close association with membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about protein structure and behavior.

claim: APP is a protein with structural similarities to type I transmembrane receptors, that might act as a cell surface receptor.
source: Furthermore, both peptides can bind APP, a protein with structural similarities to type I transmembrane receptors, that might act as a cell surface receptor.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about APP structure and involves speculative reasoning about its function.

claim: BACE1-deficient mice are susceptible to the synapto-toxicity of oAβ and oTau in a similar fashion as WT littermates.
source: We found that BACE1-deficient mice are susceptible to the synapto-toxicity of oAβ and oTau in a similar fashion as WT littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological recordings in BACE1-KO mice (Figure 5E-F).

claim: Amyloidogenic APP cleavage is not required for the impairment of LTP by the oligomers.
source: Thus, amyloidogenic APP cleavage is not required for the impairment of LTP by the oligomers.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that BACE1-KO mice are susceptible to oAβ and oTau toxicity (Figure 5E-F).

claim: The APP dependence for the negative effect of oAβ and oTau onto LTP is specific to these proteins.
source: We also found that the APP dependence for the negative effect of oAβ and oTau onto LTP is specific to these proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that oAmy impairs LTP in APP-KO mice (Figure 5G).

claim: The finding that Aβ and Tau share APP as a common mechanism for impairing LTP and memory is relevant and provides a common etiopathogenetic mechanism for their involvement in AD.
source: Regardless, the finding that Aβ and Tau share APP as a common mechanism for impairing LTP and memory is relevant and provides a common etiopathogenetic mechanism for their involvement in AD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and involves speculative reasoning about disease mechanisms.

claim: The data are consistent with the hypothesis that APP serves as a common, direct molecular target for extracellular oAβ and oTau to impair LTP and memory.
source: Our data are consistent with the hypothesis that APP serves as a common, direct molecular target for extracellular oAβ and oTau to impair LTP and memory.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing APP-dependence of oAβ and oTau toxicity.

claim: Both oAβ and oTau bind to APP.
source: This is supported by the demonstration that both oAβ and oTau bind to APP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation and far-Western blot experiments (Figure 1).

claim: The experiments do not conclusively demonstrate that oligomer binding to APP is the cause of LTP and memory reduction.
source: However, our experiments do not conclusively demonstrate that oligomer binding to APP is the cause of LTP and memory reduction, nor we can rigorously exclude the possibility that the two types of oligomers act on additional targets.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the limitations of the experimental approach.

claim: Heparan sulfate and heparin sulphate proteoglycans bind with Aβ and Tau.
source: For instance, it has been demonstrated that heparan sulfate and heparin sulphate proteoglycans bind with Aβ and Tau (Holmes et al., 2013; Lindahl et al., 2009) and mediate their internalization and neurotoxicity (Holmes et al., 2013; Mirbaha et al., 2015; Sandwall et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Holmes et al., 2013; Lindahl et al., 2009).

claim: Heparan sulfate and heparin sulphate proteoglycans mediate the internalization and neurotoxicity of Aβ and Tau.
source: For instance, it has been demonstrated that heparan sulfate and heparin sulphate proteoglycans bind with Aβ and Tau (Holmes et al., 2013; Lindahl et al., 2009) and mediate their internalization and neurotoxicity (Holmes et al., 2013; Mirbaha et al., 2015; Sandwall et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Holmes et al., 2013; Mirbaha et al., 2015; Sandwall et al., 2010).

claim: APP and heparan sulfate proteoglycans are likely to interact at the plasma membrane.
source: Given that APP and heparan sulfate proteoglycans are likely to interact at the plasma membrane (Reinhard et al., 2013) and proteoglycans are rapidly degraded in the absence of proteins belonging to the APP superfamily (Cappai et al., 2005) proteoglycan degradation in the absence of APP might block the toxic action of oAβ and oTau.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Reinhard et al., 2013).

claim: Proteoglycans are rapidly degraded in the absence of proteins belonging to the APP superfamily.
source: Given that APP and heparan sulfate proteoglycans are likely to interact at the plasma membrane (Reinhard et al., 2013) and proteoglycans are rapidly degraded in the absence of proteins belonging to the APP superfamily (Cappai et al., 2005) proteoglycan degradation in the absence of APP might block the toxic action of oAβ and oTau.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Cappai et al., 2005).

claim: Proteoglycan degradation in the absence of APP might block the toxic action of oAβ and oTau.
source: Given that APP and heparan sulfate proteoglycans are likely to interact at the plasma membrane (Reinhard et al., 2013) and proteoglycans are rapidly degraded in the absence of proteins belonging to the APP superfamily (Cappai et al., 2005) proteoglycan degradation in the absence of APP might block the toxic action of oAβ and oTau.
evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning based on inference from cited literature.

claim: Extracellular oAβ and oTau disrupt molecular mechanisms of synaptic plasticity and memory via APP.
source: Nevertheless, the main observation of this manuscript showing that extracellular oAβ and oTau disrupt molecular mechanisms of synaptic plasticity and memory via APP is clear and has relevant implications for understanding AD etiopathogenesis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing APP-dependence of oAβ and oTau toxicity.

claim: Suppression of APP reduces oAβ and oTau entrance into cells.
source: We have found that suppression of APP reduces oAβ and oTau entrance into cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 2).

claim: Intracellular perfusion with 6E10 antibodies recognizing the sequence 1–16 of human Aβ42, rescues the LTP block by extracellular human oAβ.
source: This observation combined with the finding that intracellular perfusion with 6E10 antibodies recognizing the sequence 1–16 of human Aβ42, rescues the LTP block by extracellular human oAβ (Ripoli et al., 2014), supports the hypothesis that, at least for oAβ, APP-dependent uploading of extracellular oligomers plays a critical role the impairment of synaptic plasticity, and presumably memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Ripoli et al., 2014).

claim: For oAβ, APP-dependent uploading of extracellular oligomers plays a critical role in the impairment of synaptic plasticity, and presumably memory.
source: This observation combined with the finding that intracellular perfusion with 6E10 antibodies recognizing the sequence 1–16 of human Aβ42, rescues the LTP block by extracellular human oAβ (Ripoli et al., 2014), supports the hypothesis that, at least for oAβ, APP-dependent uploading of extracellular oligomers plays a critical role the impairment of synaptic plasticity, and presumably memory.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and citation to previous literature (Ripoli et al., 2014).

claim: APP might permit the entrance of the peptides into cells either directly into the cytosol or within vesicles during endocytosis.
source: APP might permit the entrance of the peptides into cells either directly into the cytosol or within vesicles during endocytosis, after which molecular mechanisms of learning and memory are impaired.
evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms.

claim: A direct entrance into the cytosol might occur if APP functions as a channel through which the two oligomers both with a diameter in the low nm range enter cells.
source: A direct entrance into the cytosol might occur if APP functions as a channel through which the two oligomers both with a diameter in the low nm range (Cizas et al., 2010; Fá et al., 2016) enter cells.
evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms and is supported by citations about oligomer size (Cizas et al., 2010; Fá et al., 2016).

claim: APP forms a non-selective channel when injected in Xenopus oocytes.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, it has been reported that APP forms a non-selective channel when injected in Xenopus oocytes (Fraser et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Fraser et al., 1996).

claim: APP permits the formation of pores/channels by the oligomers, as ion conductance across lipid bilayers is increased by oligomers of several different amyloids.
source: A variant on this hypothesis is that APP permits the formation of pores/channels by the oligomers, as ion conductance across lipid bilayers is increased by oligomers of several different amyloids (Kayed et al., 2004), which affect the permeability of the plasma membrane, leading to elevation of intracellular [Ca2+] and toxic changes.
evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms and is supported by citation to previous literature (Kayed et al., 2004).

claim: Aβ has been reported to form large conductance, non-specific ion channels.
source: With this regard, Aβ has been reported to form large conductance, non-specific ion channels (Fraser et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Fraser et al., 1997).

claim: Full-length APP is a transmembrane protein, which is endocytosed from the cell surface into endosomes.
source: The endocytotic mechanism, in turn, is supported by the demonstration that full-length APP is a transmembrane protein, which is endocytosed from the cell surface into endosomes (Nordstedt et al., 1993) and by studies showing endocytosis of Tau (Wu et al. 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Nordstedt et al., 1993).

claim: Studies show endocytosis of Tau.
source: The endocytotic mechanism, in turn, is supported by the demonstration that full-length APP is a transmembrane protein, which is endocytosed from the cell surface into endosomes (Nordstedt et al., 1993) and by studies showing endocytosis of Tau (Wu et al. 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Wu et al. 2013).

claim: APP suppression does not dramatically affect the number of MAP2-positive cells taking up Aβ (only ~80% of WT cells), but does reduce the number of intracellular aggregates for the peptide per neuron (~55% of WT cells).
source: Another aspect of our experiments is that APP suppression does not appear to dramatically affect the number of MAP2-positive cells taking up Aβ (only ~80% of WT cells), but does reduce the number of intracellular aggregates for the peptide per neuron (~55% of WT cells), whereas APP suppression clearly affects both the number of cells taking up Tau (~50%) and the number of intracellular aggregates for oTau (~52%).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: APP suppression clearly affects both the number of cells taking up Tau (~50%) and the number of intracellular aggregates for oTau (~52%).
source: Another aspect of our experiments is that APP suppression does not appear to dramatically affect the number of MAP2-positive cells taking up Aβ (only ~80% of WT cells), but does reduce the number of intracellular aggregates for the peptide per neuron (~55% of WT cells), whereas APP suppression clearly affects both the number of cells taking up Tau (~50%) and the number of intracellular aggregates for oTau (~52%).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The number of cells taking up oligomers and the amount of intracellular aggregates may reflect two different processes, i.e., uptake and degradation/clearance of aggregates.
source: These findings open the question of whether the number of cells taking up oligomers and the amount of intracellular aggregates may reflect two different processes, i.e., uptake and degradation/clearance of aggregates.
evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: To date there is no data showing that APP is involved in modulation of Aβ/Tau clearance.
source: Of note, to date there is no data showing that APP is involved in modulation of Aβ/Tau clearance.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about the current state of the literature.

claim: Oligomer interaction with APP might activate the intracellular segment of APP, AID/AICD, triggering a cascade of events leading to derangement of memory mechanisms.
source: Albeit the experiments on oligomer entrance support the hypothesis that APP serves as a Trojan horse for oAβ and oTau to enter neurons prior to impairing second messenger cascades relevant to synaptic plasticity and memory formation, they do not exclude an alternative scenario in which oligomer interaction with APP activates the intracellular segment of APP, AID/AICD, triggering a cascade of events leading to derangement of memory mechanisms.
evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Phosphorylation of the intracellular threonine 668 of APP mediates synaptic plasticity deficits and memory loss.
source: In support of this hypothesis, it has been shown that phosphorylation of the intracellular threonine 668 of APP mediates synaptic plasticity deficits and memory loss (Lombino et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Lombino et al., 2013).

claim: The AID/AICD fragment of APP could form a multimeric complex with the nuclear adaptor protein Fe65 and the histone acetyltransferase Tip60, potentially stimulating transcription.
source: Moreover, the AID/AICD fragment of APP could form a multimeric complex with the nuclear adaptor protein Fe65 and the histone acetyltransferase Tip60, potentially stimulating transcription (Cao and Südhof, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Cao and Südhof, 2001).

claim: Tau entrance leads to propagation of Tau misfolding.
source: If so, the entrance of the oligomers might serve other purposes rather than impairing synaptic plasticity and memory. For instance, it has been suggested that Tau entrance leads to propagation of Tau misfolding (Frost et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Frost et al., 2009).

claim: APP is necessary for impairment of LTP and memory following elevation of Aβ and Tau.
source: Nevertheless, our findings that APP is necessary for impairment of LTP and memory following elevation of Aβ and Tau is still relevant, as it sheds light into how the oligomers cause memory loss in AD and other neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing APP-dependence of oAβ and oTau toxicity.

claim: The prevailing hypothesis in the AD field is that Aβ triggers Tau pathology.
source: The prevailing hypothesis in the AD field is that Aβ triggers Tau pathology.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about the current state of the AD field.

claim: The data do not support the hypothesis in which Aβ and Tau are placed in series but suggest a different scenario in which extracellular Aβ and Tau oligomers act in parallel, both through APP.
source: Our data, however, do not support this hypothesis in which Aβ and Tau are placed in series but suggest a different scenario in which extracellular Aβ and Tau oligomers act in parallel, both through APP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that both oAβ and oTau require APP for their toxic effects.

claim: This hypothesis would explain why tauopathies result in neuronal loss similar to AD but in the absence of Aβ.
source: Interestingly, this hypothesis would also explain why tauopathies result in neuronal loss similar to AD but in the absence of Aβ.
evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The findings are translationally significant, as they have permitted the identification of a common molecule, APP, which might be therapeutically targeted.
source: Nevertheless, our findings are translationally significant, as they have permitted the identification of a common molecule, APP, which might be therapeutically targeted at sites serving for direct interaction with Aβ and Tau oligomers or, alternatively, with proteins downstream of such oligomers, other than the classical β- and γ-secretase sites.
evidence: This claim involves speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic applications based on the experimental findings.
